CausalChain: High-temperature brewing conditions -> increased formation of reactive catechin quinones -> accumulation of quinone metabolites in green tea infusion -> selective induction of pro-oxidative stress in cancer stem cells (which have limited antioxidant enzyme capacity) -> apoptosis of cancer stem cells -> reduction in tumor renewal and metastasis
Hypothesis: Green tea catechins, when prepared under high-temperature brewing conditions, generate reactive quinone metabolites that selectively trigger apoptosis in cancer stem cells, thereby reducing tumor recurrence and metastasis, and this effect may be harnessed to augment standard cancer therapies.
Abstract: Recent observations suggest that modifications in standard green tea preparation methods, particularly high‐temperature brewing, may lead to the formation of reactive catechin quinone metabolites that selectively induce apoptosis in cancer stem cells. In this hypothesis, we propose that specific brewing conditions enhance the pro-oxidative properties of green tea catechins, producing quinones that overwhelm the limited antioxidant defenses of cancer stem cells. This selective cytotoxicity might reduce tumor renewal and metastasis while sparing normal cells. The potential synergism with standard chemo- and immunotherapies offers a novel adjunct approach for targeting aggressive and therapy-resistant cancer cell populations.
